course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 4
unit.description: Follow the rise of party politics and a more participatory democracy, the market revolution, westward expansion and foreign policy, the Second Great Awakening and reform, and the growth of slavery from 1800 to 1848.

firstTopic.title: Contextualizing Period 4
firstTopic.summary: The context for Period 4: a more participatory democracy and a new national culture, an economy transformed by innovation, and a nation that expanded westward and argued over slavery, 1800–1848.

topic.title: Market Revolution: Society and Culture
topic.summary: How the market revolution moved people to cities and to the West, divided Americans into new economic classes, and changed the roles of women and families.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes the largest groups of immigrants to the United States in the 1830s and 1840s?
choices: Italian and Eastern European immigrants who found jobs in steel mills and mines
Irish and German immigrants, many of whom settled in Northern cities
Chinese and Japanese immigrants who settled in the mining towns of California
Spanish and Portuguese immigrants who settled on the plantations of the Deep South
questions.explanation: The potato famine and economic hardship sent many Irish to Northern cities, while many Germans moved to cities and farmland in the Midwest.
choiceExplanations: Those groups arrived in large numbers after 1880.
The potato famine and economic hardship sent many Irish to Northern cities, while many Germans moved to cities and farmland in the Midwest.
Large Chinese migration began with the Gold Rush after 1848.
Few immigrants went to plantation districts.
questions.distinguisher: The Italian choice is close because Italians also immigrated in great numbers, but their main migration came later.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains the rapid growth of river cities such as Cincinnati and St. Louis?
choices: River trade carried the crops and goods of the West to distant markets
The federal government moved its offices there to be nearer to the frontier
Railroads from the East had replaced river travel by the time these cities were founded
Southern planters moved there to build textile mills on the Ohio and Mississippi
questions.explanation: Steamboats and river trade linked western farms with markets, and the towns along the rivers prospered.
choiceExplanations: Steamboats and river trade linked western farms with markets, and the towns along the rivers prospered.
The capital stayed in Washington.
River trade was the main form of transport in these decades.
The cities grew with river trade and western settlement.
questions.distinguisher: The railroads choice is close because railroads later became important, but river trade came first.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The workers recruited to the Lowell mills in the 1820s and 1830s were mainly
choices: Irish immigrant families who lived in towns owned by the mill companies
enslaved laborers hired from Southern planters to work in the Northern mills
skilled craftsmen who owned their own shops and sold cloth to the mill owners
young unmarried women from New England farms who lived in company boardinghouses
questions.explanation: Mill owners recruited young farm women, who earned cash wages and lived under supervision in boardinghouses.
choiceExplanations: Irish workers became numerous in the mills later, in the 1840s.
The Lowell mills used wage labor, not slave labor.
The mills employed wage earners and not independent craftsmen.
Mill owners recruited young farm women, who earned cash wages and lived under supervision in boardinghouses.
questions.distinguisher: The Irish families choice is close because Irish workers later filled the mills, but the first Lowell workers were native-born farm women.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was an effect of the growth of manufacturing on American society?
choices: The difference between rich and poor narrowed as every worker gained the same wage
Most Americans left the cities to farm, because factory wages could not support a family
A larger middle class and a wealthy elite grew alongside a large group of laboring poor
Craftsmen and their apprentices grew in number as factories closed in most towns
questions.explanation: Manufacturing raised living standards for some while many workers earned low wages in crowded conditions.
choiceExplanations: Wealth and living standards became more unequal.
Cities and factory work grew.
Manufacturing raised living standards for some while many workers earned low wages in crowded conditions.
Factories multiplied, and many craft workers lost their independence.
questions.distinguisher: The narrowing choice is close because wages rose for some workers, but class divisions widened.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why more Americans supported themselves by making goods for distant markets?
choices: A decline in the price of farmland made small farms unprofitable in every region
Better transportation and factories made it practical to sell goods far away
A federal law required families to sell what they made in markets and not at home
A ban on imports left Americans without any other source of cloth, tools, or shoes
questions.explanation: Transportation and factories reduced costs, and families who could earn cash wages or sell goods no longer depended on semi-subsistence farming.
choiceExplanations: Farmland remained available, and prices did not end family farming.
Transportation and factories reduced costs, and families who could earn cash wages or sell goods no longer depended on semi-subsistence farming.
No such law was passed.
Imports continued during these decades.
questions.distinguisher: The farmland choice is close because some families left farms for work elsewhere, but the main cause was the growth of markets.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The ideal sometimes called the cult of domesticity held that
choices: women should be moral guardians of the home while men worked in the public sphere
women and men should share equally in paid work and in public office
families should produce most of the goods that they used inside the home
women should manage factories while men took charge of caring for children
questions.explanation: The ideal emphasized the separation of public and private spheres and gave women moral authority in the home.
choiceExplanations: The ideal emphasized the separation of public and private spheres and gave women moral authority in the home.
The ideal separated the roles of women and men.
The ideal arose as work moved out of the home.
The ideal assigned childcare to women.
questions.distinguisher: The equal-roles choice is close because the women's rights movement made such claims, but the cult of domesticity did not.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference between the lives of middle-class and working-class women in the 1840s?
choices: Middle-class women worked in factories, while working-class women stayed at home to raise children
Working-class women could vote in state elections, while middle-class women could not
Middle-class women owned most of the nation's factories, while working-class women did not
Middle-class women were expected to stay home, while many working-class women earned wages
questions.explanation: The domestic ideal described the middle class, and women who were poor, immigrant, or enslaved usually had to work.
choiceExplanations: The roles were reversed.
No women could vote in this period.
Men owned nearly all factories.
The domestic ideal described the middle class, and women who were poor, immigrant, or enslaved usually had to work.
questions.distinguisher: The reversed-roles choice is close because it uses the same terms, but wage work was more common for working-class women.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: The formation of trade unions and the ruling in Commonwealth v. Hunt (1842) are best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: The spread of slavery into the Northern states and the demand for Black labor
A decline in the number of factories that left most workers unemployed
The growth of wage labor and the problems of long hours and low pay
A federal ban on all strikes that unions challenged in the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Wage workers formed unions to seek better pay and shorter hours, and the Massachusetts court ruled that unions were lawful.
choiceExplanations: Slavery was ending in the North.
Factories were multiplying.
Wage workers formed unions to seek better pay and shorter hours, and the Massachusetts court ruled that unions were lawful.
The ruling came from a state court, and there was no federal ban on strikes.
questions.distinguisher: The slavery choice is close because labor was a topic of reform, but unions arose from wage work.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a reaction of many native-born Protestants to the growth of immigration in the 1830s and 1840s?
choices: A campaign to open the nation's borders and grant all newcomers immediate voting rights
Nativism, including hostility to Catholics and the formation of anti-immigrant groups
Support for the Catholic Church as a leader of the reform movements of the era
A law passed by Congress limiting immigration from Ireland and Germany
questions.explanation: Nativists feared the Catholic faith and the competition of immigrant workers, and they formed groups and sometimes rioted.
choiceExplanations: Most reactions were hostile and not welcoming.
Nativists feared the Catholic faith and the competition of immigrant workers, and they formed groups and sometimes rioted.
Many Protestants distrusted the Catholic Church.
Congress did not restrict immigration at this time.
questions.distinguisher: The immigration law choice is close because nativists wanted limits, but Congress did not pass them in these decades.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.
